The scored earth told him something had changed.

Luca crouched at the edge of the grove, fourteen years old and certain of very little except what the ground beneath his feet could show him. Three days ago, after the storm that had broken across the Pollino peaks with the force of divine anger, he'd come here as he came most days—to move the sheep, to check the water source, to sit in the shade of the old Bosnian pine that rose like a weathered sentinel above the limestone scattered across the hillside. The tree had always been here, longer than the village had kept its records. Longer, he suspected, than anyone living could remember.

But three days ago, something about it had shifted.

The roots, which he'd memorized over countless visits the way another boy might memorize the names of saints, no longer lay in their familiar pattern. The northern anchor, the one that had always pressed deepest into the scored stone, had moved. Not much. Perhaps a hand's breadth. But it had moved, and the earth around it bore the evidence—raw limestone scratched pale where the roots had torn free, a subtle depression where they had previously settled, and that scored earth, that fresh destruction of the orderly arrangement he had always seen.

He'd said nothing to anyone. Not yet.

The tree itself rose before him now, its dark needles absorbing the thin autumn light. The trunk was ancient, gnarled with centuries of weather, its bark thick and furrowed enough that a man could hide his fingers in the cracks. The resin had wept from several places on the south face, dark and glossy now that it had dried, crusted like old blood.

Luca placed his palm against the bark.

It was warm. Not from the sunlight—the afternoon was cooling, and the sun sat low enough that the grove was mostly shadow. The warmth came from within, steady and deliberate, pulsing very faintly beneath his hand like a heartbeat that had nothing to do with flesh or blood.

He jerked his hand away.

The tree was a tree. Trees did not move. Trees did not have heartbeats. Trees did not leave scored earth and torn roots and evidence of displacement that a shepherd boy could read like scripture written in stone and soil.

He stood, suddenly aware that his legs had begun to shake. The slopes around him were empty—the sheep were grazing two hundred paces down the hill, and no one else came to this part of the Pollino except the monks from the lower monastery when they needed medicinal herbs. Still, he felt watched. The feeling was not new to the mountains; a man who lived among rock and wind learned early to sense the attentiveness of the landscape. But this felt different. This felt like being observed by something that was aware of his observation.

Luca turned and walked back down to the sheep. His usual practice was to spend most of his time in the grove, reading the weather in the wind and the ground, letting the animals drift where they would. Today, he drove them farther down the slope, toward the lower pasture where the grass was thinner but where, at least, he could not see the old tree against the sky.

He returned the next morning.

The displacement had grown. The root system, which had always seemed almost deliberately anchored to catch water from multiple sources, had rearranged itself further. The northern anchor had moved again, just slightly, but definitely. And the soil where the roots had been was disturbed—not dramatically, not in a way that would be obvious to a casual observer, but the pattern was wrong. The displacement was coherent. It was directional.

It was as though the tree was moving deliberately northward.

Luca told himself this was impossible. He was a shepherd, not a scholar. He knew animals and weather and the behavior of plants well enough to predict the seasons and read the health of grazing land, but he understood that knowledge was a small thing, contained within the narrow bounds of practical necessity. Whatever was happening here fell outside those bounds entirely.

He came back the next day. And the next. Each time, the evidence accumulated. The roots had progressed further north, and the soil bore the marks of deliberate repositioning. The tree's lean had changed minutely, as though its center of gravity was slowly shifting. The resin weeping from the south face had increased—he could see the trail of it now, dark and thick, running down the bark like a scar.

His father noticed his absences first.

"You're spending too much time in the high pasture," his father said on the fifth day, when Luca returned to the village near dusk, having spent nearly the entire day in the grove. "The sheep don't need that much watching. They need watching, but not that much."

"The grass is better up there," Luca said, which was true. It was also only a partial truth.

"The grass was fine last month," his father replied. His father was a practical man, concerned with practicalities—the movement of animals, the management of land, the simple transactions that kept a shepherd's life moving forward. He had no patience for nuance. "Your mother is beginning to think you're not interested in the village anymore."

Luca had no response to that. His mother had always been more perceptive than his father, and if she was already noticing his pattern, it would not be long before more people began to wonder why a shepherd boy was spending so much time alone in the high Pollino, away from the established routes and the common grazing areas.

Still, he went back.

By the eighth day, the tree's movement had become undeniable. The trunk itself had shifted position, leaning more distinctly toward the north and slightly west. The roots had spread in that direction, seeking something—new soil, new water sources, new mineral composition in the limestone. The resin weeping had become profuse, dark streams running down the bark, pooling at the base where the roots met the earth. When Luca touched it, it was hot, almost uncomfortably so, and it left a sticky residue on his fingers that smelled of something acrid and resinous, unfamiliar.

It was during his observation of this resin—crouching at the base of the tree, carefully examining the fluid and trying to determine what might cause such profuse weeping—that he first became aware of being watched.

The awareness arrived without warning. Luca was entirely focused on the resin, on running his fingers along the texture of the pooled liquid, on trying to parse some meaning from the tree's visible distress. And then, as suddenly as thought arriving unbidden, he understood that someone was looking at him.

He straightened so quickly that his vision momentarily blurred. The slopes around the grove were empty. He could see the entire approach from above, the paths that descended from the higher peaks toward the monastery lands, the broader route that led toward the village. All empty. Only the wind moved across the stone, carrying the particular scent of high autumn, cold and dry and faintly resinous.

But the sensation did not fade. Someone was watching him from concealment, with the kind of patient attention that suggested long, steady observation.

Luca gathered himself deliberately. He was fourteen, which meant he was old enough to manage sheep and young enough to be entirely conscious of his vulnerability in the mountains. There were stories about the high Pollino, stories that circulated in the village in the evening, about men who had ventured into the peaks and never returned, about bandits and monks and other creatures whose names were never spoken plainly.

He walked back toward the village slowly, trying not to appear alarmed. Behind him, the old tree stood in its altered position, still weeping resin, still impossibly moved from where it had always been.

He did not return for two days. His father had noticed his absences too directly, and his mother had begun asking pointed questions about his time in the hills. Instead, Luca worked the lower pastures, herding sheep through the thinning grass, trying not to think about roots and resin and the sensation of being observed by something he could not see.

On the third day, the pressure of not knowing became unbearable. He rose before dawn, told his parents he was taking the sheep to the northern grazing area, and climbed back toward the grove.

The tree had moved again. This time, the displacement was so significant that he could not dismiss it as the work of weather or imagination. The trunk leaned noticeably farther to the north. The root system had spread in that direction with clear intention, and fresh earth was disturbed in a pattern that suggested methodical relocation. The resin had stopped weeping quite so profusely, but it had hardened in dark, glossy trails down the bark, marking the path of the weeping like a record of pain or effort.

Luca stood before the tree for a long time, trying to reconcile what he was seeing with what he understood to be possible. The tree was moving. It was moving deliberately, methodically, in a northward direction. It was moving, and this movement was impossible, which meant either that he was experiencing some form of profound delusion, or that the world contained mysteries that extended far beyond the reasonable boundaries of a shepherd boy's understanding.

He was still standing there, hand raised to the bark, when the voice spoke behind him.

"You've noticed."

Luca spun so quickly that he nearly fell. The man standing at the edge of the grove was perhaps fifty years old, though the light was uncertain and his weathered face made his actual age difficult to determine. He was dressed in the rough wool of a mountain monk, and his dark hair was streaked with gray. But it was his hands that caught Luca's attention—they bore old scarring, glossy and pale against his weathered skin, the kind of scarring that suggested electrical injury or severe burning.

"I've been watching you watch it," the man continued. His voice was low and practical, neither kind nor unkind, simply stating fact. "For eight days now. You come, you look, you touch the bark, you try to understand what you're seeing. You do it quietly, which is good. Quietly is important."

Luca's mouth was dry. "What is it?" he asked. "What is the tree?"

The man was silent for a long moment. He looked past Luca at the old pine, examining it with the kind of attention that suggested he had seen it many times before, in many different conditions.

"What does your father do?" the man asked finally.

"He's a shepherd," Luca said.

"And before that, his father?"

"Also a shepherd," Luca said. "My family has been here for... a long time."

"Yes," the man said. "You're rooted here. You understand land and animals and how the seasons work. You're beginning to understand that some things don't fit into those patterns. That's the question you're asking yourself now, isn't it? How something like that—" he gestured toward the tree with one scarred hand, "—can exist when it contradicts everything you know."

"Can you explain it?" Luca asked. He heard his own voice shake slightly.

"No," the man said simply. "Not in a way that would matter. But I can tell you this: it's not the kind of thing you ask questions about in the village. It's not the kind of thing you mention to your family, or to the monks, or to anyone else. It's the kind of thing you keep to yourself, and you learn to see without drawing attention to what you're seeing."

"Why?" Luca asked.

"Because people fear what they don't understand," the man said. "And fear makes them dangerous. If people understood what that tree is, what it can do, what it means—they would try to destroy it, or control it, or study it until it died from too much attention. The only thing that keeps it safe is silence. The only thing that keeps you safe, if you intend to stay near it, is learning to be silent too."

Luca swallowed. "Why are you telling me this? If silence is so important, why are you speaking to me now?"

"Because you've already seen it," the man said. "And you'll keep coming back. Your curiosity is the kind that won't be satisfied by leaving it alone. I can tell. I was like that once." He paused, and for just a moment, his expression shifted to something that might have been sadness or memory or both. "I could pretend I haven't seen you, let you figure out your own way to conceal what you know, hope you don't draw attention to yourself through clumsiness. Or I can tell you the only thing that matters: if you intend to come here, if you intend to keep watching and learning, you need a reason that will convince your family, a reason that makes sense."

"What reason?" Luca asked.

"Prayer," the man said. "Tell them you've taken to praying in the high places. That it's brought you closer to God, or that you believe God speaks more clearly in the mountains than in the village. Most monks are sympathetic to that kind of thing. Your family might be too, eventually. And prayer is something you can do alone, something that requires no witnesses, something that explains long absences without requiring explanation. You can pray for hours and no one will question why."

The man turned to leave, then paused. "My name is Farovald," he said. "If you see me again, be careful not to acknowledge me. We don't know each other. We've never spoken."

"Wait—" Luca said, but the man was already moving back down the slope, his movement surprisingly efficient for someone his apparent age. Within moments, he had disappeared into the rocks and scrub vegetation, and Luca was alone in the grove again with the tree and the weight of what he had just learned.

He stood there for a long time, hand on the warm bark, feeling the steady pulse of something moving beneath the skin of wood and resin. Then he turned and walked back down the mountain.

## The Storm Before

Two hundred years earlier, in the year 589 of the Christian calendar, the Pollino Mountains held a secret that neither the Lombards nor the few remaining Byzantine settlers could have imagined.

The lightning had come with a storm that bent the peaks like grass in wind. Rain fell in sheets thick enough to blind, and the lightning tracked from cloud to earth with a frequency that made the entire landscape flicker between visibility and darkness, between the world as it appeared in daylight and the world stripped down to bone and shadow.

The old Bosnian pine had stood in that place for centuries, its roots deep in the mineral-rich limestone, its connection to the soil absolute and unchanging. It was the kind of tree that a man might pass a dozen times in a life and never truly see—old enough to be invisible, established enough to seem permanent, the sort of landmark that becomes part of the landscape rather than an object within it.

The lightning struck it directly.

The electrical force traveled through the mature wood, through the cambium where growth happened cell by cell, through the root system that reached into the limestone and the specialized fungal network that had evolved alongside it for millennia. The strike left scars—darkened wood, burned bark, resin weeping from wounds that would never fully heal. The force of the electricity restructured the cellular tissue of the root system at a microscopic level, loosening the rigid connections that bound the tree to immobility, introducing a kind of electrochemical malleability into structures that had always been designed for permanence.

And in the moment of the strike, a man who had been sheltering beneath the tree—seeking protection from the rain on a route that should have avoided the storm but had not—felt the same lightning pass through him. His hands, placed against the bark when the strike came, received the full force of the electrical burn. His body, already sensitive to the earth's electrical currents in ways that would not be understood for another thousand years, underwent a transformation that would alter the remaining centuries of his life.

The man's name was Farovald, and he was thirty-nine years old when the lightning made him something other than mortal.

He staggered away from the tree when the strike ended, his burned hands hanging useless at his sides, his body convulsing with the aftereffects of the electricity. He did not understand what had happened to him. He could not have understood it—the mechanisms were too far beyond the knowledge of his time, too deeply embedded in the biology of specialized adaptation that would only be discovered and named centuries later.

But he understood that he had been touched by something vast and terrible, that it had rewritten some essential part of him, and that whatever had happened in that moment would color the remainder of his existence in ways he could not yet begin to comprehend.

The tree, in its own way, understood much the same thing.

For two hundred years, Italus and Farovald would exist in a strange parallel existence, never truly together but fundamentally connected by the singularity of that moment. The tree would learn, very slowly, to move through the soil and stone of the Pollino. The man would learn, even more slowly, that aging had become optional, that his body would repair itself from injuries that should have been fatal, that the decades would stretch out before him in a way that no other human would ever experience.

And the secret of that moment, that shared transformation, would be kept by both of them in the only way such secrets could be kept—through silence, through concealment, through the careful management of knowledge and the deliberate construction of distance from the understanding of ordinary men.

The storm passed, as all storms do. The lightning moved on to strike other peaks, other trees, other lives that it would alter without intention or malice. The rain eased and eventually ceased. The clouds broke, and the Pollino emerged again into daylight, changed in some ways and entirely unchanged in others.

A man walked down from the mountains with burned hands and no explanation for them, and a tree began, so slowly that centuries would pass before the change became truly evident, to move.

Luca did not sleep much that night. He lay on his pallet in the corner of his family's small stone house and listened to the sounds of the village settling into darkness. His father's snoring from the inner room. The dogs moving restlessly in the yard. The sound of wind in the eaves, bringing with it the scent of autumn and stone and distant resin.

He understood, in the way that young people sometimes understand things without being taught them, that he had crossed some kind of threshold. That the world he inhabited before this moment—the simple world of seasons and animals and the repetitive work that filled a shepherd's days—was no longer entirely real to him. He had seen something that should not exist, and he had been told by a stranger with burned hands and old eyes that the only appropriate response was silence.

Silence and prayer.

The next morning, before his family rose, Luca went to his mother.

"I've been thinking about taking up prayer," he told her. "More seriously. The monks say God speaks more clearly in the high places."

His mother looked at him with an expression that contained both surprise and something like satisfaction. She was a woman of faith, or at least of the practical faith that one maintained in a small village where the alternative to faith was to confront the randomness and violence of existence directly.

"That's good," she said. "The monks will help you. You can go to the monastery, ask for guidance. They like young people who are serious about their faith."

His father, when told, simply grunted acknowledgment. Prayer was not something he was interested in, but it was not something he would forbid either. If his son wanted to spend time with monks and in contemplative practice, it was a respectable use of a young man's time.

And so Luca began his first practice of concealment.

He would rise early, tell his family he was going to the high pastures, and walk instead toward the monastery. Sometimes he did actually visit the monks, listening to their teachings about the nature of God and the soul and the proper way to conduct a Christian life. Mostly, though, he would turn off the main path before reaching the monastery and climb higher into the Pollino, toward the grove and the tree that was, impossibly, learning to move.

He studied the displacement patterns with the focus of a scholar, though he was no scholar. He noted the direction of movement, the speed at which the roots progressed, the way the trunk's lean shifted with the seasons. He began to understand, through close observation, something of the mechanism by which the tree accomplished its slow relocation—the way the roots that served as anchors would tighten, creating tension, then release, and the trunk would settle slightly into a new position. The resin would bleed, the roots would rest, and then the process would begin again.

He never saw Farovald again during those early years, though he became aware of being watched occasionally, a presence in the mountains that observed his observation but never made itself known. The man had given him one piece of advice, and Luca had made it his philosophy: he kept silent. He asked no questions in the village about moving trees or strange men with burned hands. He did not discuss what he saw, even with himself, except in the form of the careful records he began to keep, hidden in a small leather journal that he carried in his pack.

These records were written in a kind of shorthand, using symbols and abbreviated phrases that would mean nothing to anyone who happened to discover them. He recorded the position of the roots, the angle of the trunk's lean, the presence or absence of resin weeping. He recorded the dates, the weather, the patterns he observed. He was constructing a record of something that should not be recordable, something that existed outside the ordinary boundaries of natural law.

He was, without knowing it, beginning the practice that would define his entire life. He was becoming a guardian, taking on the responsibility of witnessing and maintaining the secret of a tree that moved and a transformation that could not be explained.

The years passed.

Luca grew older. His voice deepened. His shoulders broadened from the work of herding and climbing. His knowledge of the mountains expanded from the areas around the village to more distant peaks, more remote valleys. And all the while, the tree continued its slow progression northward, and Luca continued to watch, to record, to maintain his silence.

He never spoke of it to anyone. Not his parents, not the monks, not the other shepherd boys who occasionally ventured into the high pastures. The secret became so much a part of him that he sometimes forgot it was a secret at all. It simply became his life—a hidden life alongside the visible one, a current running beneath the surface of his days that no one else could perceive.

Until the day, many years later, when he would discover that others had been keeping the same silence, had been guarding the same secret, and that the responsibility he had assumed alone would, eventually, need to be shared.

But that was still in the future. For now, in the cool darkness of autumn, with the Pollino settling into winter and the evidence of the tree's movement hidden beneath snow that would erase the scored earth, Luca lay awake and understood that he had been chosen for something, though he did not yet understand what, or why, or for how long the burden would rest upon his shoulders.

## The Storm Before

Two hundred years earlier, in the year 589 of the Christian calendar, the Pollino Mountains held a secret that neither the Lombards nor the few remaining Byzantine settlers could have imagined.

The lightning had come with a storm that bent the peaks like grass in wind. Rain fell in sheets thick enough to blind, and the lightning tracked from cloud to earth with a frequency that made the entire landscape flicker between visibility and darkness, between the world as it appeared in daylight and the world stripped down to bone and shadow.

The old Bosnian pine had stood in that place for centuries, its roots deep in the mineral-rich limestone, its connection to the soil absolute and unchanging. It was the kind of tree that a man might pass a dozen times in a life and never truly see—old enough to be invisible, established enough to seem permanent, the sort of landmark that becomes part of the landscape rather than an object within it.

The lightning struck it directly.

The electrical force traveled through the mature wood, through the cambium where growth happened cell by cell, through the root system that reached into the limestone and the specialized fungal network that had evolved alongside it for millennia. The strike left scars—darkened wood, burned bark, resin weeping from wounds that would never fully heal. The force of the electricity restructured the cellular tissue of the root system at a microscopic level, loosening the rigid connections that bound the tree to immobility, introducing a kind of electrochemical malleability into structures that had always been designed for permanence.

And in the moment of the strike, a man who had been sheltering beneath the tree—seeking protection from the rain on a route that should have avoided the storm but had not—felt the same lightning pass through him. His hands, placed against the bark when the strike came, received the full force of the electrical burn. His body, already sensitive to the earth's electrical currents in ways that would not be understood for another thousand years, underwent a transformation that would alter the remaining centuries of his life.

The man's name was Farovald, and he was thirty-nine years old when the lightning made him something other than mortal.

He staggered away from the tree when the strike ended, his burned hands hanging useless at his sides, his body convulsing with the aftereffects of the electricity. He did not understand what had happened to him. He could not have understood it—the mechanisms were too far beyond the knowledge of his time, too deeply embedded in the biology of specialized adaptation that would only be discovered and named centuries later.

But he understood that he had been touched by something vast and terrible, that it had rewritten some essential part of him, and that whatever had happened in that moment would color the remainder of his existence in ways he could not yet begin to comprehend.

The tree, in its own way, understood much the same thing.

For two hundred years, Italus and Farovald would exist in a strange parallel existence, never truly together but fundamentally connected by the singularity of that moment. The tree would learn, very slowly, to move through the soil and stone of the Pollino. The man would learn, even more slowly, that aging had become optional, that his body would repair itself from injuries that should have been fatal, that the decades would stretch out before him in a way that no other human would ever experience.

And the secret of that moment, that shared transformation, would be kept by both of them in the only way such secrets could be kept—through silence, through concealment, through the careful management of knowledge and the deliberate construction of distance from the understanding of ordinary men.

The storm passed, as all storms do. The lightning moved on to strike other peaks, other trees, other lives that it would alter without intention or malice. The rain eased and eventually ceased. The clouds broke, and the Pollino emerged again into daylight, changed in some ways and entirely unchanged in others.

A man walked down from the mountains with burned hands and no explanation for them, and a tree began, so slowly that centuries would pass before the change became truly evident, to move.

Luca did not sleep much that night. He lay on his pallet in the corner of his family's small stone house and listened to the sounds of the village settling into darkness. His father's snoring from the inner room. The dogs moving restlessly in the yard. The sound of wind in the eaves, bringing with it the scent of autumn and stone and distant resin.

He understood, in the way that young people sometimes understand things without being taught them, that he had crossed some kind of threshold. That the world he inhabited before this moment—the simple world of seasons and animals and the repetitive work that filled a shepherd's days—was no longer entirely real to him. He had seen something that should not exist, and he had been told by a stranger with burned hands and old eyes that the only appropriate response was silence.

Silence and prayer.

The next morning, before his family rose, Luca went to his mother.

"I've been thinking about taking up prayer," he told her. "More seriously. The monks say God speaks more clearly in the high places."

His mother looked at him with an expression that contained both surprise and something like satisfaction. She was a woman of faith, or at least of the practical faith that one maintained in a small village where the alternative to faith was to confront the randomness and violence of existence directly.

"That's good," she said. "The monks will help you. You can go to the monastery, ask for guidance. They like young people who are serious about their faith."

His father, when told, simply grunted acknowledgment. Prayer was not something he was interested in, but it was not something he would forbid either. If his son wanted to spend time with monks and in contemplative practice, it was a respectable use of a young man's time.

And so Luca began his first practice of concealment.

He would rise early, tell his family he was going to the high pastures, and walk instead toward the monastery. Sometimes he did actually visit the monks, listening to their teachings about the nature of God and the soul and the proper way to conduct a Christian life. Mostly, though, he would turn off the main path before reaching the monastery and climb higher into the Pollino, toward the grove and the tree that was, impossibly, learning to move.

He studied the displacement patterns with the focus of a scholar, though he was no scholar. He noted the direction of movement, the speed at which the roots progressed, the way the trunk's lean shifted with the seasons. He began to understand, through close observation, something of the mechanism by which the tree accomplished its slow relocation—the way the roots that served as anchors would tighten, creating tension, then release, and the trunk would settle slightly into a new position. The resin would bleed, the roots would rest, and then the process would begin again.

He never saw Farovald again during those early years, though he became aware of being watched occasionally, a presence in the mountains that observed his observation but never made itself known. The man had given him one piece of advice, and Luca had made it his philosophy: he kept silent. He asked no questions in the village about moving trees or strange men with burned hands. He did not discuss what he saw, even with himself, except in the form of the careful records he began to keep, hidden in a small leather journal that he carried in his pack.

These records were written in a kind of shorthand, using symbols and abbreviated phrases that would mean nothing to anyone who happened to discover them. He recorded the position of the roots, the angle of the trunk's lean, the presence or absence of resin weeping. He recorded the dates, the weather, the patterns he observed. He was constructing a record of something that should not be recordable, something that existed outside the ordinary boundaries of natural law.

He was, without knowing it, beginning the practice that would define his entire life. He was becoming a guardian, taking on the responsibility of witnessing and maintaining the secret of a tree that moved and a transformation that could not be explained.

The years passed.

Luca grew older. His voice deepened. His shoulders broadened from the work of herding and climbing. His knowledge of the mountains expanded from the areas around the village to more distant peaks, more remote valleys. And all the while, the tree continued its slow progression northward, and Luca continued to watch, to record, to maintain his silence.

He never spoke of it to anyone. Not his parents, not the monks, not the other shepherd boys who occasionally ventured into the high pastures. The secret became so much a part of him that he sometimes forgot it was a secret at all. It simply became his life, one that  was a hidden life alongside the visible one, a current running beneath the surface of his days that no one else could perceive.

Until the day, many years later, when he would discover that others had been keeping the same silence, had been guarding the same secret, and that the responsibility he had assumed alone would, eventually, need to be shared.

But that was still in the future. For now, in the cool darkness of autumn, with the Pollino settling into winter and the evidence of the tree's movement hidden beneath snow that would erase the scored earth, Luca lay awake and understood that he had been chosen for something, though he did not yet understand what, or why, or for how long the burden would rest upon his shoulders.
